questions.prompt:
A sample of an element contains isotopes of mass numbers 24, 25 and 26. Their percentage abundances are 78.7%, 10.1% and 11.2% respectively (ignore any isotope with 0%).
(a) Calculate the relative atomic mass of the sample. (3)
(b) Explain why isotopes of the same element have almost identical chemical properties. (2)
(c) Describe how first ionisation energy generally changes across a period and explain the trend. (5)
hints: Use a weighted mean for isotopic abundance.
Chemical behaviour is controlled mainly by electrons.
For periodic trends compare nuclear charge, shielding and distance.
questions.solution:
(a) Weighted mean $A_r=\dfrac{\sum(m\times\%abundance)}{100}\approx 24.325$.
(b) Isotopes have the same proton number and therefore the same electron configuration, so they form the same types of bonds and react similarly.
(c) Across a period nuclear charge increases while shielding changes relatively little; atomic radius decreases and the attraction between the nucleus and the outer electron increases, so first ionisation energy generally increases (allowing for subshell/pairing anomalies).

questions.inspiredBy: OCR A Level Chemistry B (Salters) H433/03, June 2025 - paper-aligned practice set, slot 5

questions.prompt:
The complete combustion of methane has $\Delta H_c^\circ=-890$ kJ mol$^{-1}$.
(a) State what is meant by standard enthalpy change of combustion. (2)
(b) A burner transfers 45% of the released energy to 0.500 kg of water. Calculate the temperature rise when 0.0200 mol of fuel is burned. Use $c=4.18$ J g$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$. (4)
(c) Explain, in terms of bond breaking and bond making, why combustion is exothermic. (4)
hints: Convert kJ to J before using q=mcΔT.
Apply the stated efficiency.
Compare total energy for bonds broken and formed.
questions.solution:
(a) Enthalpy change when one mole of substance is completely burned in oxygen under standard conditions, with substances in their standard states.
(b) Useful energy $=8010$ J. $\Delta T=q/(mc)=3.83$ K.
(c) Bond breaking requires energy and bond formation releases energy; in combustion, formation of strong C=O and O-H bonds releases more energy than is required to break bonds in the reactants.

questions.prompt:
The complete combustion of propane has $\Delta H_c^\circ=-2220$ kJ mol$^{-1}$.
(a) State what is meant by standard enthalpy change of combustion. (2)
(b) A burner transfers 55% of the released energy to 0.500 kg of water. Calculate the temperature rise when 0.0200 mol of fuel is burned. Use $c=4.18$ J g$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$. (4)
(c) Explain, in terms of bond breaking and bond making, why combustion is exothermic. (0)
hints: Convert kJ to J before using q=mcΔT.
Apply the stated efficiency.
Compare total energy for bonds broken and formed.
questions.solution:
(a) Enthalpy change when one mole of substance is completely burned in oxygen under standard conditions, with substances in their standard states.
(b) Useful energy $=24420$ J. $\Delta T=q/(mc)=11.68$ K.
(c) Bond breaking requires energy and bond formation releases energy; in combustion, formation of strong C=O and O-H bonds releases more energy than is required to break bonds in the reactants.

questions.prompt:
The complete combustion of propane has $\Delta H_c^\circ=-2220$ kJ mol$^{-1}$.
(a) State what is meant by standard enthalpy change of combustion. (2)
(b) A burner transfers 55% of the released energy to 0.500 kg of water. Calculate the temperature rise when 0.0200 mol of fuel is burned. Use $c=4.18$ J g$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$. (4)
(c) Explain, in terms of bond breaking and bond making, why combustion is exothermic. (5)
hints: Convert kJ to J before using q=mcΔT.
Apply the stated efficiency.
Compare total energy for bonds broken and formed.
questions.solution:
(a) Enthalpy change when one mole of substance is completely burned in oxygen under standard conditions, with substances in their standard states.
(b) Useful energy $=24420$ J. $\Delta T=q/(mc)=11.68$ K.
(c) Bond breaking requires energy and bond formation releases energy; in combustion, formation of strong C=O and O-H bonds releases more energy than is required to break bonds in the reactants.

questions.prompt:
The complete combustion of propane has $\Delta H_c^\circ=-2220$ kJ mol$^{-1}$.
(a) State what is meant by standard enthalpy change of combustion. (2)
(b) A burner transfers 55% of the released energy to 0.500 kg of water. Calculate the temperature rise when 0.0200 mol of fuel is burned. Use $c=4.18$ J g$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$. (4)
(c) Explain, in terms of bond breaking and bond making, why combustion is exothermic. (4)
hints: Convert kJ to J before using q=mcΔT.
Apply the stated efficiency.
Compare total energy for bonds broken and formed.
questions.solution:
(a) Enthalpy change when one mole of substance is completely burned in oxygen under standard conditions, with substances in their standard states.
(b) Useful energy $=24420$ J. $\Delta T=q/(mc)=11.68$ K.
(c) Bond breaking requires energy and bond formation releases energy; in combustion, formation of strong C=O and O-H bonds releases more energy than is required to break bonds in the reactants.

questions.prompt:
The complete combustion of propane has $\Delta H_c^\circ=-2220$ kJ mol$^{-1}$.
(a) State what is meant by standard enthalpy change of combustion. (2)
(b) A burner transfers 55% of the released energy to 0.500 kg of water. Calculate the temperature rise when 0.0200 mol of fuel is burned. Use $c=4.18$ J g$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$. (4)
(c) Explain, in terms of bond breaking and bond making, why combustion is exothermic. (0)
hints: Convert kJ to J before using q=mcΔT.
Apply the stated efficiency.
Compare total energy for bonds broken and formed.
questions.solution:
(a) Enthalpy change when one mole of substance is completely burned in oxygen under standard conditions, with substances in their standard states.
(b) Useful energy $=24420$ J. $\Delta T=q/(mc)=11.68$ K.
(c) Bond breaking requires energy and bond formation releases energy; in combustion, formation of strong C=O and O-H bonds releases more energy than is required to break bonds in the reactants.

questions.prompt:
The complete combustion of propane has $\Delta H_c^\circ=-2220$ kJ mol$^{-1}$.
(a) State what is meant by standard enthalpy change of combustion. (2)
(b) A burner transfers 55% of the released energy to 0.500 kg of water. Calculate the temperature rise when 0.0200 mol of fuel is burned. Use $c=4.18$ J g$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$. (4)
(c) Explain, in terms of bond breaking and bond making, why combustion is exothermic. (6)
hints: Convert kJ to J before using q=mcΔT.
Apply the stated efficiency.
Compare total energy for bonds broken and formed.
questions.solution:
(a) Enthalpy change when one mole of substance is completely burned in oxygen under standard conditions, with substances in their standard states.
(b) Useful energy $=24420$ J. $\Delta T=q/(mc)=11.68$ K.
(c) Bond breaking requires energy and bond formation releases energy; in combustion, formation of strong C=O and O-H bonds releases more energy than is required to break bonds in the reactants.

questions.prompt:
The complete combustion of propane has $\Delta H_c^\circ=-2220$ kJ mol$^{-1}$.
(a) State what is meant by standard enthalpy change of combustion. (2)
(b) A burner transfers 55% of the released energy to 0.500 kg of water. Calculate the temperature rise when 0.0200 mol of fuel is burned. Use $c=4.18$ J g$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$. (4)
(c) Explain, in terms of bond breaking and bond making, why combustion is exothermic. (4)
hints: Convert kJ to J before using q=mcΔT.
Apply the stated efficiency.
Compare total energy for bonds broken and formed.
questions.solution:
(a) Enthalpy change when one mole of substance is completely burned in oxygen under standard conditions, with substances in their standard states.
(b) Useful energy $=24420$ J. $\Delta T=q/(mc)=11.68$ K.
(c) Bond breaking requires energy and bond formation releases energy; in combustion, formation of strong C=O and O-H bonds releases more energy than is required to break bonds in the reactants.

questions.prompt:
Aqueous chlorine chemistry can be represented using redox half-equations.
(a) Define oxidation in terms of electrons. (1)
(b) Write a reduction half-equation for $X_2$ forming $X^-$ ions. (2)
(c) The standard electrode potential for $X_2/2X^-$ is +1.36 V. Explain how electrode potentials can be used to predict whether a halogen displacement reaction is feasible. (3)
(d) In an electrolysis experiment, 0.250 mol of electrons pass through a molten halide. Calculate the amount of $X_2$ formed. (6)
hints: Remember OIL RIG.
Balance atoms first, then charge with electrons.
Two electrons are involved per halogen molecule.
questions.solution:
(a) Oxidation is loss of electrons.
(b) $X_2+2e^-\rightarrow2X^-$.
(c) Combine reduction potentials so that the more positive half-cell is reduced; a positive overall $E^\circ_{cell}$ indicates thermodynamic feasibility under standard conditions.
(d) Two moles of electrons correspond to one mole of halogen, so 0.250 mol e$^-$ gives 0.125 mol $X_2$.

questions.prompt:
A simplified atmospheric reaction has rate equation $\text{rate}=k[A][B]$, where $k=0.012$ dm$^3$ mol$^{-1}$ s$^{-1}$.
(a) State the overall order of the reaction. (1)
(b) Calculate the initial rate when $[A]=0.20$ and $[B]=0.15$ mol dm$^{-3}$. (2)
(c) Explain how a catalyst changes the rate constant at a fixed temperature. (2)
(d) Describe the initiation and propagation ideas in a free-radical chain mechanism involving UV light. (6)
hints: Add the powers in the rate equation for overall order.
Substitute concentrations directly into the rate equation.
Radical mechanisms use single-electron species.
questions.solution:
(a) Overall order = 2.
(b) Rate $=(0.012)(0.20)(0.15)=0.00036$ mol dm$^{-3}$ s$^{-1}$.
(c) A catalyst provides an alternative pathway with lower activation energy, so a larger fraction of collisions is successful and the effective rate constant is larger.
(d) Initiation uses UV energy for homolytic bond fission to form radicals. Propagation steps consume a radical and form another radical so the chain continues; termination removes radicals by combination.

A simplified atmospheric reaction has rate equation $\text{rate}=k[A][B]$, where $k=0.025$ dm$^3$ mol$^{-1}$ s$^{-1}$.
(a) State the overall order of the reaction. (1)
(b) Calculate the initial rate when $[A]=0.30$ and $[B]=0.10$ mol dm$^{-3}$. (2)
(c) Explain how a catalyst changes the rate constant at a fixed temperature. (2)
(d) Describe the initiation and propagation ideas in a free-radical chain mechanism involving UV light. (6)
hints: Add the powers in the rate equation for overall order.
Substitute concentrations directly into the rate equation.
Radical mechanisms use single-electron species.
questions.solution:
(a) Overall order = 2.
(b) Rate $=(0.025)(0.30)(0.10)=0.00075$ mol dm$^{-3}$ s$^{-1}$.
(c) A catalyst provides an alternative pathway with lower activation energy, so a larger fraction of collisions is successful and the effective rate constant is larger.
(d) Initiation uses UV energy for homolytic bond fission to form radicals. Propagation steps consume a radical and form another radical so the chain continues; termination removes radicals by combination.

(a) State the overall order of the reaction. (1)
(b) Calculate the initial rate when $[A]=0.20$ and $[B]=0.15$ mol dm$^{-3}$. (2)
(c) Explain how a catalyst changes the rate constant at a fixed temperature. (2)
(d) Describe the initiation and propagation ideas in a free-radical chain mechanism involving UV light. (5)
hints: Add the powers in the rate equation for overall order.
Substitute concentrations directly into the rate equation.
Radical mechanisms use single-electron species.
questions.solution:
(a) Overall order = 2.
(b) Rate $=(0.012)(0.20)(0.15)=0.00036$ mol dm$^{-3}$ s$^{-1}$.
(c) A catalyst provides an alternative pathway with lower activation energy, so a larger fraction of collisions is successful and the effective rate constant is larger.
(d) Initiation uses UV energy for homolytic bond fission to form radicals. Propagation steps consume a radical and form another radical so the chain continues; termination removes radicals by combination.

questions.prompt:
An organic compound used in a synthesis is identified as an ester.
(a) State an infrared absorption that would support this identification; a strong absorption is observed near 1740 cm$^{-1}$. (2)
(b) Explain why IR spectroscopy is useful for identifying functional groups but may not uniquely identify a compound. (2)
(c) Describe how reflux differs from distillation in an organic preparation. (3)
(d) Suggest two features of a synthesis that would make it 'greener'. (5)
hints: Use characteristic bond absorptions rather than memorising whole spectra.
Think about what happens to condensed vapour in reflux.
Green chemistry reduces waste, hazard and energy use.
questions.solution:
(a) Match the observed wavenumber to the characteristic bond: carbonyl groups absorb strongly near 1700–1750 cm$^{-1}$; O-H absorptions are broad at higher wavenumber.
(b) Functional groups give characteristic absorptions, but different molecules can contain the same groups; the fingerprint region is needed for stronger identification.
(c) In reflux, vapour is condensed and returned to the reaction vessel, allowing prolonged heating without loss of volatile reagents. In distillation, vapour is condensed and collected separately.
(d) Valid improvements include higher atom economy, safer/renewable solvents, catalytic rather than stoichiometric reagents, lower energy use, reduced toxicity and reduced waste.

questions.paper: OCR Chemistry B (Salters) H433/03 - Practical skills in chemistry
questions.inspiredBy: OCR A Level Chemistry B (Salters) H433/03, June 2025 - paper-aligned practice set, slot 7

questions.prompt:
An industrial equilibrium has equilibrium constant $K_c=4.0$ at 450 K.
(a) Write the general expression for $K_c$ for $aA+bB\rightleftharpoons cC+dD$. (2)
(b) Explain what a large value of $K_c$ indicates about the equilibrium composition. (2)
(c) Explain why a catalyst does not change $K_c$. (2)
(d) Discuss two compromises that may be made when choosing industrial temperature and pressure. (4)
hints: Products appear in the numerator of Kc.
Catalysts affect kinetics, not the equilibrium constant.
Industrial conditions balance rate, yield, cost and safety.
questions.solution:
(a) $K_c=\dfrac{[C]^c[D]^d}{[A]^a[B]^b}$.
(b) A large $K_c$ indicates products are favoured at equilibrium, subject to the stoichiometric powers.
(c) A catalyst speeds up forward and reverse reactions by the same kinetic route and does not change the thermodynamic equilibrium position.
(d) Higher temperature often increases rate but may reduce equilibrium yield for an exothermic reaction; higher pressure may favour the side with fewer gas molecules but raises compression/equipment costs and safety demands.

(a) Write the general expression for $K_c$ for $aA+bB\rightleftharpoons cC+dD$. (2)
(b) Explain what a large value of $K_c$ indicates about the equilibrium composition. (2)
(c) Explain why a catalyst does not change $K_c$. (2)
(d) Discuss two compromises that may be made when choosing industrial temperature and pressure. (4)
hints: Products appear in the numerator of Kc.
Catalysts affect kinetics, not the equilibrium constant.
Industrial conditions balance rate, yield, cost and safety.
questions.solution:
(a) $K_c=\dfrac{[C]^c[D]^d}{[A]^a[B]^b}$.
(b) A large $K_c$ indicates products are favoured at equilibrium, subject to the stoichiometric powers.
(c) A catalyst speeds up forward and reverse reactions by the same kinetic route and does not change the thermodynamic equilibrium position.
(d) Higher temperature often increases rate but may reduce equilibrium yield for an exothermic reaction; higher pressure may favour the side with fewer gas molecules but raises compression/equipment costs and safety demands.

questions.paper: OCR Chemistry B (Salters) H433/03 - Practical skills in chemistry
questions.inspiredBy: OCR A Level Chemistry B (Salters) H433/03, June 2025 - paper-aligned practice set, slot 8

questions.prompt:
A short peptide contains amino acids joined by peptide bonds.
(a) State the type of reaction by which two amino acids form a peptide bond. (1)
(b) Draw or describe the functional group present in a peptide link. (2)
(c) Explain why changes in pH can alter the tertiary structure of a protein. (3)
(d) A proton NMR spectrum contains signals with relative areas 3:2:1. Explain what integration tells you and give one limitation of using integration alone to identify a structure. (5)
hints: A peptide bond forms with loss of a small molecule.
Protein structure depends on interactions between side chains.
NMR integration is about relative proton counts.
questions.solution:
(a) Condensation.
(b) The peptide link contains $-C(=O)-NH-$.
(c) pH changes protonation of acidic/basic side chains, changing ionic attractions and hydrogen-bonding patterns; this can alter folding and therefore the active three-dimensional structure.
(d) Integration gives relative numbers of protons in different chemical environments. It does not by itself identify which groups those protons belong to; chemical shifts, splitting and other data are also needed.

questions.inspiredBy: OCR A Level Chemistry B (Salters) H433/02, June 2025 - paper-aligned practice set, slot 7

questions.prompt:
A weak monoprotic acid has concentration 0.100 mol dm$^{-3}$ and $K_a=1.8e-05$.
(a) Write an expression for $K_a$. (2)
(b) Assuming the acid is only slightly dissociated, calculate the pH. (4)
(c) Explain how adding its conjugate base can make a buffer solution. (2)
(d) Explain qualitatively how increasing atmospheric CO$_2$ can lower ocean pH. (4)
hints: For a weak acid, use the small-dissociation approximation.
pH = -log10[H+].
A buffer needs a weak acid/base and its conjugate partner.
questions.solution:
(a) $K_a=\dfrac{[H^+][A^-]}{[HA]}$.
(b) For small dissociation, $[HA]\approx0.100$ and $[H^+]\approx[A^-]$. Thus $[H^+]=\sqrt{K_aC}=0.00134$ mol dm$^{-3}$, so pH $=2.872$.
(c) A weak acid/conjugate-base pair removes added $H^+$ or $OH^-$ and therefore resists pH change.
(d) Dissolved CO$_2$ forms carbonic-acid species; equilibria produce additional $H^+$, lowering pH.

questions.inspiredBy: OCR A Level Chemistry B (Salters) H433/03, June 2023 - paper-aligned practice set, slot 1

questions.prompt:
A weak monoprotic acid has concentration 0.050 mol dm$^{-3}$ and $K_a=1.3e-05$.
(a) Write an expression for $K_a$. (2)
(b) Assuming the acid is only slightly dissociated, calculate the pH. (4)
(c) Explain how adding its conjugate base can make a buffer solution. (2)
(d) Explain qualitatively how increasing atmospheric CO$_2$ can lower ocean pH. (-2)
hints: For a weak acid, use the small-dissociation approximation.
pH = -log10[H+].
A buffer needs a weak acid/base and its conjugate partner.
questions.solution:
(a) $K_a=\dfrac{[H^+][A^-]}{[HA]}$.
(b) For small dissociation, $[HA]\approx0.050$ and $[H^+]\approx[A^-]$. Thus $[H^+]=\sqrt{K_aC}=0.000806$ mol dm$^{-3}$, so pH $=3.094$.
(c) A weak acid/conjugate-base pair removes added $H^+$ or $OH^-$ and therefore resists pH change.
(d) Dissolved CO$_2$ forms carbonic-acid species; equilibria produce additional $H^+$, lowering pH.

questions.prompt:
Two standard reduction half-cells have potentials +0.34 V and +1.23 V.
(a) Calculate the standard cell potential for the spontaneous combination. (2)
(b) State which half-cell is reduced. (1)
(c) Explain why a positive $E^\circ_{cell}$ does not guarantee a rapid reaction. (2)
(d) Describe how a calibration graph can be used to determine the concentration of a coloured transition-metal ion by colorimetry. (6)
hints: More positive reduction potential is the cathode process.
Use Ecell = Ecathode - Eanode.
Colorimetry needs standards and a calibration plot.
questions.solution:
(a) The more positive half-cell is the reduction: $E^\circ_{cell}=1.23-(0.34)=0.89$ V.
(b) The half-cell with +1.23 V is reduced.
(c) Electrode potentials describe thermodynamic feasibility, not activation energy or reaction mechanism; a feasible reaction may be kinetically slow.
(d) Measure absorbance for standards of known concentration at a suitable wavelength, plot absorbance against concentration, measure the unknown under the same conditions and interpolate its concentration from the calibration line.

questions.inspiredBy: OCR A Level Chemistry B (Salters) H433/01, June 2024 - paper-aligned practice set, slot 2

questions.prompt:
Two standard reduction half-cells have potentials +-0.14 V and +0.80 V.
(a) Calculate the standard cell potential for the spontaneous combination. (2)
(b) State which half-cell is reduced. (1)
(c) Explain why a positive $E^\circ_{cell}$ does not guarantee a rapid reaction. (2)
(d) Describe how a calibration graph can be used to determine the concentration of a coloured transition-metal ion by colorimetry. (5)
hints: More positive reduction potential is the cathode process.
Use Ecell = Ecathode - Eanode.
Colorimetry needs standards and a calibration plot.
questions.solution:
(a) The more positive half-cell is the reduction: $E^\circ_{cell}=0.80-(-0.14)=0.94$ V.
(b) The half-cell with +0.80 V is reduced.
(c) Electrode potentials describe thermodynamic feasibility, not activation energy or reaction mechanism; a feasible reaction may be kinetically slow.
(d) Measure absorbance for standards of known concentration at a suitable wavelength, plot absorbance against concentration, measure the unknown under the same conditions and interpolate its concentration from the calibration line.

questions.paper: OCR Chemistry B (Salters) H433/03 - Practical skills in chemistry
questions.inspiredBy: OCR A Level Chemistry B (Salters) H433/03, June 2025 - paper-aligned practice set, slot 10

questions.prompt:
A coloured organic compound contains an aromatic ring and a conjugated system.
(a) Explain why extended conjugation can lead to absorption in the visible region. (3)
(b) Describe how an azo dye can be formed from a diazonium ion and an activated aromatic ring. (3)
(c) In TLC, a spot moves 4.2 cm while the solvent front moves 7.0 cm. Calculate the $R_f$ value. (2)
(d) State one reason why TLC alone may not prove the identity of a compound. (3)
hints: Visible colour is linked to electronic transitions.
Azo coupling forms an N=N link between aromatic systems.
Rf = distance moved by solute / distance moved by solvent front.
questions.solution:
(a) Conjugation produces delocalised electrons and reduces the energy separation between relevant electronic levels; photons in the visible range can then promote electronic transitions.
(b) A diazonium ion acts as an electrophile and couples with an activated aromatic ring, forming an $-N=N-$ azo link while retaining an extended conjugated system.
(c) $R_f=4.2/7.0=0.60$.
(d) Different substances can have similar $R_f$ values; identity should be supported by standards and/or other analytical data.

questions.inspiredBy: OCR A Level Chemistry B (Salters) H433/03, June 2025 - paper-aligned practice set, slot 1

questions.prompt:
A student titrates 25.0 cm$^3$ of an analyte with 0.1000 mol dm$^{-3}$ reagent. The mean titre is 24.60 cm$^3$ and the stoichiometric ratio is 1:1.
(a) Calculate the amount, in moles, of reagent used. (2)
(b) Calculate the analyte concentration. (2)
(c) Explain why concordant titres are required. (1)
(d) Suggest improvements that reduce random error and one safety precaution. (1)
hints: Convert cm3 to dm3.
Use the mole ratio before calculating concentration.
Distinguish repeatability from systematic error.
questions.solution:
(a) $n=cV=(0.1000)(0.02460)=0.00246$ mol.
(b) At 1:1 ratio the analyte amount is the same, so $c=n/V=0.0984$ mol dm$^{-3}$.
(c) Concordant results show repeatability and reduce the influence of random variation.
(d) Repeat titrations, use a white tile, add titrant dropwise near the end point, read the meniscus at eye level, and use suitable eye protection for corrosive/irritant reagents.

questions.prompt:
A student titrates 25.0 cm$^3$ of an analyte with 0.1000 mol dm$^{-3}$ reagent. The mean titre is 24.60 cm$^3$ and the stoichiometric ratio is 1:1.
(a) Calculate the amount, in moles, of reagent used. (2)
(b) Calculate the analyte concentration. (2)
(c) Explain why concordant titres are required. (1)
(d) Suggest improvements that reduce random error and one safety precaution. (1)
hints: Convert cm3 to dm3.
Use the mole ratio before calculating concentration.
Distinguish repeatability from systematic error.
questions.solution:
(a) $n=cV=(0.1000)(0.02460)=0.00246$ mol.
(b) At 1:1 ratio the analyte amount is the same, so $c=n/V=0.0984$ mol dm$^{-3}$.
(c) Concordant results show repeatability and reduce the influence of random variation.
(d) Repeat titrations, use a white tile, add titrant dropwise near the end point, read the meniscus at eye level, and use suitable eye protection for corrosive/irritant reagents.

questions.prompt:
A student titrates 25.0 cm$^3$ of an analyte with 0.0800 mol dm$^{-3}$ reagent. The mean titre is 18.75 cm$^3$ and the stoichiometric ratio is 1:1.
(a) Calculate the amount, in moles, of reagent used. (2)
(b) Calculate the analyte concentration. (2)
(c) Explain why concordant titres are required. (1)
(d) Suggest improvements that reduce random error and one safety precaution. (1)
hints: Convert cm3 to dm3.
Use the mole ratio before calculating concentration.
Distinguish repeatability from systematic error.
questions.solution:
(a) $n=cV=(0.0800)(0.01875)=0.0015$ mol.
(b) At 1:1 ratio the analyte amount is the same, so $c=n/V=0.06$ mol dm$^{-3}$.
(c) Concordant results show repeatability and reduce the influence of random variation.
(d) Repeat titrations, use a white tile, add titrant dropwise near the end point, read the meniscus at eye level, and use suitable eye protection for corrosive/irritant reagents.

questions.prompt:
Read this short scientific passage:

A research team is investigating battery recycling. The process could improve recovery of lithium and transition metals, but its environmental benefit depends on energy demand, raw materials and the lifetime of the equipment. Measurements from a pilot plant show that increasing temperature improves rate but also increases energy use.

(a) Identify two claims in the passage that would require quantitative evidence before a firm conclusion could be made. (2)
(b) Explain the difference between correlation and causation in evaluating the temperature data. (2)
(c) Suggest two additional measurements that would help assess the sustainability of the process. (2)
(d) Write a balanced scientific conclusion that acknowledges uncertainty. (4)
hints: Separate observations from claims.
Correlation alone does not establish a mechanism.
A good conclusion states limitations and uncertainty.
questions.solution:
(a) Examples include the claimed environmental benefit and the trade-off between increased rate and increased energy demand.
(b) Correlation means variables change together; causation requires evidence that changing one variable is responsible for the change in the other, with confounding variables controlled.
(c) Suitable measurements include energy per mole/product mass, greenhouse-gas emissions, material recovery yield, waste production, water use, equipment lifetime or uncertainty/repeatability data.
(d) A sound conclusion weighs benefits against measured costs, states whether the evidence supports the claim, and explicitly notes uncertainty and limits of extrapolating pilot-scale results.

(c) Suggest two additional measurements that would help assess the sustainability of the process. (2)
(d) Write a balanced scientific conclusion that acknowledges uncertainty. (0)
hints: Separate observations from claims.
Correlation alone does not establish a mechanism.
A good conclusion states limitations and uncertainty.
questions.solution:
(a) Examples include the claimed environmental benefit and the trade-off between increased rate and increased energy demand.
(b) Correlation means variables change together; causation requires evidence that changing one variable is responsible for the change in the other, with confounding variables controlled.
(c) Suitable measurements include energy per mole/product mass, greenhouse-gas emissions, material recovery yield, waste production, water use, equipment lifetime or uncertainty/repeatability data.
(d) A sound conclusion weighs benefits against measured costs, states whether the evidence supports the claim, and explicitly notes uncertainty and limits of extrapolating pilot-scale results.
